scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Zapin originated in the 14th to 15th centuries when Arab Muslim missionaries and traders from Hadramaut, Yemen, introduced the dance to the Malay Archipelago.
Initially a male-only religious ritual performed in courts and villages, it served as a medium for Islamic proselytisation (dakwah).
Over centuries, it evolved into a secular folk dance inclusive of female performers.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Zapin is performed during social and religious occasions including weddings, village feasts, baby hair-cutting rituals (cukur jambul), Quran recitation completion ceremonies (khatam al-Quran), and Islamic holidays such as Maulud Nabi and Hari Raya Puasa.
The dance functions as communal entertainment, social bonding, and a medium for moral and spiritual education through song lyrics and choreography.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical ensemble centers on the gambus, a short-necked lute related to the Arabic oud, which performs melodic lines and solo improvisations called taqsim.
Percussion includes marwas (small double-headed drums played in pairs), rebana (frame drums), gendang (barrel drums), and gong for accentuation.
Listen for the gambus, marwas, rebana, gendang.
The pulse is 4/4.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Male dancers traditionally wear the Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga, a collarless Malay shirt with long pants and kain samping waistcloth, topped with a songkok cap.
Female dancers wear the Baju Kurung Teluk Belanga, a modest long blouse with a sarong and selendang shawl draped over head or shoulders.
Accessories include traditional Malay jewelry such as dokoh necklaces and kerongsang brooches.

scenes.title: The people
narration: In Johor, the late Rabu bin Haron (Wak Rabu) is credited as the founder of Zapin Lenga, a foundational style of the dance.
His legacy was passed to Haji Sukur bin Basir and is currently preserved by cultural practitioner Majid bin Rawino.
Zapin exists in numerous regional variants across Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, and Singapore, each with distinct movement styles and musical accompaniments.
Zapin descends from Yemeni dance traditions brought by Hadrami traders and missionaries, blending Arab musical and dance elements with indigenous Malay culture.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Zapin is variant of Zapin Arab: Energetic, fast-paced style performed by Arab-descended communities in Johor.
Zapin is variant of Zapin Melayu Johor: Malay adaptation with controlled, refined movements.
Zapin is shares region of Mak Yong: Traditional Malay performing art from the same cultural milieu.
Zapin is shares region of Khon: Classical dance-drama from Southeast Asia, different style but regional proximity.

wardrobe.from_sources: Male dancers traditionally wear the Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga, a collarless Malay shirt with long pants and kain samping waistcloth, topped with a songkok cap. Female dancers wear the Baju Kurung Teluk Belanga, a modest long blouse with a sarong and selendang shawl draped over head or shoulders. Accessories include traditional Malay jewelry such as dokoh necklaces and kerongsang brooches. Makeup is natural and understated to complement the dance’s modest aesthetic. Performances occur at weddings, communal feasts, Quran completion ceremonies, and Islamic festivals, often in village halls, courts, or cultural stages.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Male dancers traditionally wear the Baju Melayu Teluk Belanga, a collarless Malay shirt with long pants and kain samping waistcloth, topped with a songkok cap. Female dancers wear the Baju Kurung Teluk Belanga, a modest long blouse with a sarong and selendang shawl draped over head or shoulders. Accessories include traditional Malay jewelry such as dokoh necklaces and kerongsang brooches. Makeup is natural and understated to complement the dance’s modest aesthetic. Performances occur at weddings, communal feasts, Quran completion ceremonies, and Islamic festivals, often in village halls, courts, or cultural stages.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Zapin is performed during social and religious occasions including weddings, village feasts, baby hair-cutting rituals (cukur jambul), Quran recitation completion ceremonies (khatam al-Quran), and Islamic holidays such as Maulud Nabi and Hari Raya Puasa. The dance functions as communal entertainment, social bonding, and a medium for moral and spiritual education through song lyrics and choreography. It symbolizes Malay cultural values of modesty, respect, and harmony, and serves as a cultural identity marker and tool for heritage preservation and cultural diplomacy.
